item.title: PM Carney prepared for ‘risk’ that Trump might order U.S.-led military invasion of Canada: report
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump says, 'Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country.' ...
item.dc:creator: CTVNews.ca Staff
item.content:encoded: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he’s prepared for the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report. In an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, Carney described the prospect of an invasion as an “extreme tail risk,” but that it would be “irresponsible” not to prepare. Earlier in the day, Trump said on Truth Social that “Canada is destroying itself by allowing millions and millions of people into the Country” who were “essentially unchecked and unvetted.” Meanwhile, Carney spoke in New York at a so-called “pledging event” for the OceanEye observation system, funded in large part by the European Union. Key updates: Here’s what happened on Sept. 23, 2026: Carney prepared for U.S. invasion of Canada: NYT Prime Minister Mark Carney has carefully examined the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump ordering a military invasion of Canada, according to a new report. In an interview with The New York Times released Wednesday, Carney described the prospect as an “extreme tail risk,” a term used to describe to an event that could cause enormous damage, but is unlikely enough to be overlooked. However, the prime minister explained that what he did was “just risk management.” “That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare for the possibility, Carney told The Times. Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer Canada aims to reduce reliance on U.S.: Carney In the interview with The New York Times, Carney said Canada was looking into expanding its economic ties with China and reducing both its military and technological reliance on the United States, including Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite systems. The prime minister also told the Times that in the future, with a different U.S. president, “we will be a better partner for the U.S. because of what we are doing.” Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer Canada still reviewing F-35 fighter jet order: Carney The prime minister also discussed Canada’s review of its planned order of 88 U.S. F-35 fighter jets, and the potential of instead buying Sweden’s Saab Gripen fighters. “It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of the economic return,” Carney said. Canada has already committed to buying 16 of the American F-35 fighter jets to replace the country’s aging fleet of CF-18 Hornets, but Carney ordered a review of the contract for the remaining 72 aircraft after Trump first announced tariffs on Canadian goods early last year. Earlier this month, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Ottawa was assessing all available options. Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca producer With files from Todd Coyne, CTVNewsVancouver.ca journalist Trump talks Canadian unemployment In Trump’s post, he mentioned what he called Canada’s “big” unemployment rate. “It is a Liberal takeover that will end up very badly,” he said. “Already showing up in their numbers. Big unemployment.” Canada’s unemployment rate was 6.4 per cent in August, according to the most recent labour survey from Statistics Canada. That’s more than two percentage points above the U.S. reported unemployment rate, which was 4.1 per cent in August. However, the two countries calculate unemployment differently. For example, Canada considers people who are not working because of family responsibilities as unemployed, but the U.S. does not. A TD study released in the fall of 2025 predicted the unemployment rate would have been at least one point higher if population growth had not been slowed. Unemployment is impacted by a number of factors, not limited to immigration. For example, Statistics Canada noted accelerated employment losses in trade-dependent industries following Trump’s imposition of tariffs on Canadian goods. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Data contradict Trump immigration claims As U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada is “destroying itself” with its immigration policies, new data from Statistics Canada show the number of newcomers is going down. According to Statistics Canada, Canada’s population rose slightly by 0.2 per cent in the second quarter, while immigration is down 4.2 per cent year-over-year, and the number of non-permanent residents is down 0.7 per cent. The Canadian government under former prime minister Justin Trudeau pledged to cut its immigration targets following years of criticism that they were putting too much pressure on the housing market and other sectors. In Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first budget in late 2025, the Liberals set new targets, promising to “responsibly manage immigration to alleviate pressures on housing demand.” Immigration levels in Canada reached a record high in 2024. According to the federal government, 483,640 immigrants were admitted as permanent residents that year, which was in line with targets set out in the Government of Canada’s Immigration Levels Plan at the time. In 2025, that number dropped to about 393,500 new permanent residents. Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer Anand responds to Trump Asked to respond to Trump’s comments, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said that, while immigration overall has improved “Canadian prosperity,” the federal government reduced immigration intake in 2024. “We are stabilizing immigration levels,” she said Wednesday, adding Ottawa moved to reduce levels to ensure accessibility to affordable housing and health care. Canada plans to reduce temporary resident volumes to five per cent by the end of 2027. Overall permanent resident admissions are projected to stabilize at 380,000 from 2026 to 2028, with a preference on offering status to migrants who are already in Canada with “needed skills and experience.” Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist No more Trump Avenue A street in Canada’s capital bearing the name of the current U.S. president will be renamed. Ottawa city council unanimously agreed to a motion to begin the process of renaming Trump Avenue, in Ottawa’s Central Park neighbourhood. Trump Avenue is one of several streets in Central Park that references New York City. Other street names include Madison Park, Manhattan Crescent, Bloomingdale Street, and Staten Street. At the time of the neighbourhood’s development, Trump was a famous real estate mogul, but his tumultuous time as president of the United States has led to renewed calls to take his name off street signs in the capital. Ted Raymond, CTVNewsOttawa.ca journalist. Read the full story here Carney talks bilateral collaboration Carney, who is co-hosting the OceanEye event, says the meeting is in the same spirit as his trip to Strasbourg last week, where talk of Canada’s associate EU membership made headlines worldwide. Today, he said, is all about what “nations coming together” can accomplish. He did not mention the United States in his opening remarks. He said Canada is committing $82 million to the ocean observation program, which he characterized as an imperative step for the country with the world’s longest coastline. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Canada to protect more lands and waters Carney said Canada plans to send autonomous underwater gliders on months-long assignments to monitor activity under the Arctic ice. “We can’t protect what we can’t see,” he said, adding Ottawa plans to expand protected lands and waters to two-million-square kilometres by the end of the decade. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Carney to appear with EU leader Carney will speak at the OceanEye International Alliance event at 10 a.m. EDT. The OceanEye initiative aims to build capacity for marine observance, which the European Commission says is associated with a market worth up to C$32 billion. “This serves a much larger business ecosystem worth EUR 40 to 90 billion, in which the United States holds the largest share,” reads a statement from the commission published earlier this year. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist. Read the full story here. Diana Fox Carney is Canada’s Ocean Envoy Diana Fox Carney, who’s married to Mark Carney, is Canada’s Ocean Envoy. She was named to the unpaid position in mid-September. “In this role, Mme. Fox Carney will advance Canada’s leadership by connecting ocean conservation, climate action, Indigenous leadership, economic resilience and maritime security,” reads a release announcing her appointment. Fox Carney, an economist and sustainability advisor, holds master’s degrees in agricultural economics from the University of Oxford and in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania. Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist Here’s what happened on Sept. 22, 2026: India’s Modi to visit Canada: Carney Carney confirmed on Tuesday that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be visiting Canada in December. The news was first reported by the Globe and Mail on Tuesday, citing India’s High Commissioner to Canada, who says Modi will be visiting to sign a trade deal between the two countries. “We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India,” Carney said, before confirming Modi’s mid-December visit to Canada. “It is an exceptionally important relationship on many, many levels.” Modi’s last trip to Canada was in June 2025, when he attended the G7 Summit in Kananaskis, Alta. The visit raised eyebrows at the time because of the previously strained relationship between Canada and India. The two countries had been at odds since 2023, when the federal government first levelled allegations of both foreign interference and transnational repression, including crimes such as murder and extortion. At the time, talks toward a free-trade agreement — which had been underway for years — were indefinitely put on pause, and not picked up again until Carney became prime minister. Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer Carney reacts to Trump’s Belarus potash deal Carney touched on Canada’s potash industry, after Trump revealed on Monday that the U.S. plans to buy cheaper product from Belarus. “My message to the Canadian potash industry is one of admiration,” Carney said to reporters at the UN. “Canada supplies 40 per cent of the world’s potash. It is an incredible strength of our economy.” Carney affirmed that Canadian potash would continue to be in demand around the world due to Canada being a reliable, cost-competitive supplier. The prime minister also said Canada will continue to be the largest supplier of potash to the U.S. and expressed that now is an opportunity for Canada and its neighbours to co-operate and “become fertilizer independent.” “So not just potash, but across all ammonia and other fertilizers, that would be good for Canadian farmers,” he said. “It’d be great for American farmers, and it’s an opportunity we’re prepared to explore.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist U.S. to continue buying Canadian potash: Trump Trump says his country will continue buying Canadian potash after all. Trump made the comments to reporters during a bilateral meeting at the United Nations General Assembly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “Belarus has a lot of potash, and our farmers need good prices, and we want to get a lower price,” Trump told reporters Tuesday when asked about the proposed deal. “We’ll continue to go with Canada, but Belarus would like to sell it for a much lower price.” The Canadian Press. item.title: ‘Not exactly where we want to be’: Investment strategist on Canada-U.S. relations
item.description: As Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government continues to pursue economic partnerships with countries outside the U.S., the need for Canada to reach a new trade deal with its southern neighbour is only ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: As Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government continues to pursue economic partnerships with countries outside the U.S., the need for Canada to reach a new trade deal with its southern neighbour is only intensifying, an expert says. “Every new (Canadian) trade deal seems to be bringing a certain amount of ire out of the U.S.,” Pierre Ouimet, head investment strategist at UBS Canada, told BNN Bloomberg in an interview Wednesday. “We need to negotiate something solid with the U.S. at some point in time… this whole thing just creates an environment of uncertainty and that’s not really favourable when we’re trying to attract capital from everywhere in the world.” Ouimet’s comments came after Carney announced on Tuesday that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be visiting Canada in December, when a new trade deal may be signed between Ottawa and New Delhi. “What India is looking for is energy, that’s the main thing, and they want a secure supply as well, so Canada is on the top of the list,” Ouimet said. “(It would be) another trade deal; what can I say, Mr. Carney has been pursuing trade deals left, right and centre and in the process, he keeps poking the bear, as we say.” Last week, Carney attended European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France, when she announced her intention to “open the door” for Canada to become the European Union’s (EU) first associate member. U.S. President Donald Trump said such a move could be considered a “hostile act” and threatened to increase tariffs on the EU if a formal Canada-EU partnership is forged with “bad intentions.” Tariffs not a ‘major threat’ As Canadian and U.S. negotiators remain at odds over a new trade deal, tariffs and counter-tariffs continue to weigh on Canada’s economy, but Ouimet argued that they are not “necessarily a threat” in the long term. “I think most serious people agree that tariffs are not the way to go, unless it’s really specific in some industries with some obvious abuses, but overall, tariffs and the use of tariffs… I don’t think that’s a major threat,” he said. “We’re already in the mix of it; how bad can it get? Can it really get worse?” Still, Ouimet said a prolonged trade war with Canada’s largest and most important trading partner is not ideal for the country’s economy or its financial markets. “A trade war with the U.S.,” he said, “is not exactly where we want to be.”

item.title: John Zechner’s Top Picks for Sept. 23, 2026
item.description: Half of the growth in the U.S. economy over the past year has come from the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom, and the other half has been derived by the equity wealth effect on consumer ...
item.content:encoded:
John Zechner, Chairman and Founder, J Zechner Associates Focus: North American Large Caps

Top Picks: Capital Power , Rogers Communications , Apotex Health MARKET OUTLOOK: We have a cautious investment stance. Outside of concerns about valuations and excessively bullish sentiment we are wary about the sustainability of U.S. economic growth on what we view as a ‘wobbly two-legged stool’ of growth. Half of the growth in the U.S. economy over the past year has come from the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom, and the other half has been derived by the equity wealth effect on consumer spending at the top tier. In client portfolios we added U.S. long term bonds holdings as a hedge against ongoing stock market gains as well as our expectations that economic growth is slowing down and core inflations is receding back to its target level. Gold stocks continue to be a large holding for the same reasons but also as protection against a deterioration in the U.S. dollar. We continue to hold a healthy weight in technology stocks since they are delivering the strongest earnings growth across the entire market. However, we have sold most holdings related to ongoing data centre spending and a semiconductor market where we see risks. Hyperscalers such as Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft are showing accelerating cloud computing growth at rates exceeding 50 per cent which shows how well they are monetizing their AI spending. Meanwhile, Meta stands out as a great value within the sector with 3.6 billion daily active users of its ‘family of apps’ which gives it tremendous leverage in the mobile advertising world. We continue to hold Canadian energy stocks due to their low valuation and growing favour among international investors due to geo-political stability in Canada. We sold our bank stocks in both Canada and the U.S. valuations are at excessive and unsustainable levels. Growth has been driven largely by capital markets activities, trading and wealth management, which have all been helped by strong stock markets. However, this over-dependence on continued strong markets is a concern. The consumer sector also looks to be on shaky ground, particularly with the trade war with the U.S. heating up. We prefer defensive holdings such as power utilities, alternative energy and telecom, where the valuations are at the low end of historical ranges and the dividend yields remains attractive. Market-moving news, fast:  Get the BNN Bloomberg App now Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at  bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters TOP PICKS: John Zechner's Top Picks: Capital Power, Rogers Communications & Apotex Health John Zechner, chairman and founder of J Zechner Associates, shares his top stock picks to watch in the market.

Capital Power (CPX TSX) The company Canada’s largest independent power producer, generating 12 gigawatts via a 35-plant fleet. It has most of its assets in Alberta, one of two markets in North America that are unregulated. It has great scope to add capacity to meet increasing growth of data centres in Alberta with 70 per cent being gas-fired generation and 20 per cent renewable sources, which they can then connect to the grid. They did a timely U.S. acquisition last year in the PJM region where electricity rates have recently been increased. The stock trades around nine times operating cash flow and has a 4.7 per cent dividend yield. Rogers Communications (RCI-B TSX) The telecom sector looks like it has started to turn around with wireless price competition among the four players subsiding and companies focusing solely on their core areas of strength. Rogers stands out for a number of reasons: the strength of its consolidated sports assets in a market where valuations keep increasing and the fact that it is cutting back on capex and therefore generating substantial free cash flow which will allow it to pay down the debt from the Shaw acquisition and then begin to increase its dividend again. Apotex Health (APTX TSX) We looked into the business model and results as a private company and decided to participate in the initial public offering (IPO) earlier this year. The generics business has been very profitable and the stock was priced at a very reasonable valuation. Despite the recent overhang from the secondary stock sales (private equity buyer and the Sherman family) we see strong growth going forward from branded specialty pharmaceuticals, biosimilar pharmaceuticals and their position as the only generic producer of GLP-1 drugs in Canada. The Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) Health Care index has not had a strong institutional offering in over a decade so Apotex should be able to fill this gap and continue to attract new buyers.
